title: How Far Is the Simulation From the Bench: Comparing Two Traces, and the Noise Floor No Model Can Beat

questions.question: Why is plotting the two traces on the same axes not enough?
options: A plot cannot show two traces at once
A plot rounds the values to the screen's pixels
Plots take too long to draw for long runs
It finds a gross error and misses a small one that matters, and it cannot go in a test: a model 17 percent out looks fine and scores nearly three times the noise floor
questions.explanation: A person's eye catches a model that is far out and passes one that is a little out. And nobody's eye runs in continuous integration.

questions.question: A simulated trace is 0.05 too high everywhere. What are its bias and its lag?
options: A bias of 0 and a lag of 1: an offset on a rising trace looks like a shift
A bias of 0.0500 and a lag of 0: the shift is judged by the variance of the differences, so a constant offset does not move it
A bias of 0.0500 and a lag of 5
A bias of 0 and a lag of 0: a constant does not count
questions.explanation: Shifting a rising trace moves it toward one that is too high, so plain error would report a lag of 1. Judging by how much the differences vary takes the constant out.

questions.question: A sensor is 5 samples late in an open loop. What does compare find, and what does it find inside a closed loop?
options: Open loop: shift 5 and an error of 0.0000 at it; closed loop: shift 4 and an error that barely fell, 0.1396 from 0.1553, since the controller reacts to the late reading and the dynamics change
Shift 5 and an error of 0.0000 in both
Shift 4 in both, with the error halved
Open loop: shift 0; closed loop: shift 5
questions.explanation: On its own a delay is a pure shift and is found exactly. In a loop the controller acts on the late reading, so the whole response changes and no shift lines the traces up.

questions.question: What is the noise floor, and how is it found?
options: The rms noise on one real run, found from two real runs of the same thing: their rms difference over the square root of two: 0.0102 for noise 0.01
The sensor's resolution, read from its data sheet
The smallest error any model scored
The error of the model at its best fit
questions.explanation: Two real runs differ only by their noise, and the difference of two noisy values has root two times the noise of one. No model can score below that.

questions.question: A model's time constant is 17 percent below the real motor's. What does its error look like?
options: About the floor: 0.0098, too close to tell
Nearly three times the floor: 0.0272 against 0.0098, in a loop that plots much the same
Ten times the floor
17 percent above the floor
questions.explanation: At the true time constant the error sat on the floor, 0.0098. At 0.10, where the plots look alike, it was 0.0272.

questions.question: What does the name of an exceeded limit tell you?
options: When the limit was exceeded
By how much the limit was exceeded
What to look at: a model that exceeds only lag is missing a delay, and one that exceeds rmse and max has the wrong dynamics
Which run was the simulated one
questions.explanation: The fitted model exceeded none. The one with the wrong motor and no sensor delay exceeded rmse, max and lag, and each name points at a cause.
